The First Book of Meqabyan — Complete

Orit Ge'ez Ethiopian Canon — All 36 Chapters

Meqabyan's Battle — Against Idolatry — Divine Faithfulness — Covenant Restoration

PRIMARY MANUSCRIPT AUTHORITIES

Ge'ez manuscript tradition — Ethiopian Orthodox canon

Unique to the Orit Ge'ez — Not found in any other ancient canon

No Christian theological overlay — Pre-Christian Afro-Asiatic composition

Primary witness: Ge'ez manuscripts of the Ethiopian textual tradition

COMPARATIVE NOTES AT END OF EVERY CHAPTER

DSS · ORIT GE'EZ · MASORETIC VARIANT · CRITICAL NOTE

YHWH / 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 and The Creator only — no substitute titles

INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK OF MEQABYAN

1 The Book of Meqabyan — known in Ge'ez as Meqabyan — is unique to the Ethiopian Orit canon and has no parallel in any other ancient scriptural tradition. It is one of three books bearing the Meqabyan designation and is entirely distinct from the Greek Maccabees books found in Catholic and Orthodox traditions, despite superficial name similarity.

2 The text presents a warrior named Meqabyan and his battle against idolatry and apostasy among the people of YHWH. The theological framework is consistently ancient Afro-Asiatic covenant theology: faithfulness to YHWH brings life, abandonment of YHWH brings destruction, and the covenant is ultimately inviolable because YHWH Himself upholds it.

3 The Meqabyan books circulated exclusively within the Ethiopian textual tradition and were never subjected to the Greek translation process that transformed and in places distorted other ancient Hebrew and Aramaic compositions. This makes them among the least contaminated texts in the entire corpus — preserved in Ge'ez without passing through Greek, Latin, or Syriac intermediaries.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] The Meqabyan books have no DSS attestation. They belong exclusively to the Orit Ge'ez tradition. Their absence from the DSS corpus does not diminish their textual integrity — many ancient compositions were not preserved at Qumran. The DSS corpus is large but not exhaustive of all ancient Israelite textual production.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The Meqabyan books are the most purely Ge'ez texts in the entire ancient canon — composed within the Ethiopian textual tradition, preserved in Ge'ez without intermediary translation, and never subjected to the canonization pressures that shaped the texts entering the Greek, Latin, and Syriac traditions. They represent the Afro-Asiatic covenantal wisdom tradition in its most unmediated preserved form.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] The Masoretic canon contains no equivalent to the Meqabyan books. The Masoretic tradition does not preserve any of the three Meqabyan compositions. Their complete absence from the Masoretic canon is consistent with the systematic exclusion of Afro-Asiatic textual traditions that did not pass through the Babylonian exile filtering process that shaped the Masoretic compilation.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The Meqabyan books are among the least known texts in all of ancient scripture scholarship, which is itself a product of the Western academic prioritization of Greek and Latin manuscript traditions over Ge'ez ones. The Ethiopian textual tradition is older than the Latin tradition and arguably more conservative than the Greek, yet it has received a fraction of the scholarly attention. This is a direct consequence of the colonial-era dismissal of African textual traditions as derivative or secondary.

MEQABYAN BOOK ONE — CHAPTERS 1 THROUGH 19

CHAPTER 1 — MEQABYAN RISES AGAINST IDOLATRY

1 In those days there was a man named Meqabyan, a warrior mighty in battle, who feared YHWH with all his heart. And he saw that the people of YHWH had turned from the covenant and were bowing before idols of wood and stone and had forsaken the Torah of The Creator.

2 And the heart of Meqabyan burned within him when he saw these things. And he prayed to YHWH saying: How long will You be silent, YHWH? Your people have abandoned Your covenant and no one rises to call them back. If You will be with me I will speak to them.

3 And YHWH answered Meqabyan and said: I have seen the apostasy of My people and it is an abomination before Me. Rise up and go to them and speak My words in their hearing. Do not fear their faces for I am with you.

4 And Meqabyan went to the assembly of the people and he stood in the gate of the city and he spoke in a loud voice saying: People of YHWH, hear me. How long will you limp between two opinions? If YHWH is The Creator, follow Him. If the idols are gods, follow them.

5 But the people mocked him and said: Who are you to speak to us? Are you better than we are? And some took stones to throw at him. But Meqabyan stood firm and he said: It is not I who speak to you but YHWH your Creator who has sent me.

6 And YHWH showed a sign in that hour. The idol that stood in the centre of the city fell and shattered into dust. And the people were afraid. And some of them said: Truly YHWH is The Creator and there is no other. And they returned to Him that day.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] No DSS parallel. The Meqabyan tradition is exclusive to the Orit Ge'ez corpus.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The narrative pattern of Meqabyan — a righteous warrior who rises against apostasy, is mocked and threatened, but is vindicated by YHWH's direct intervention — parallels the Eliyahu narrative tradition in the Israelite prophetic corpus. The falling of the idol echoes the Dagon narrative in Shemu'el. The Ge'ez tradition draws on these ancient Afro-Asiatic narrative patterns and applies them in a new historical context.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] The Masoretic tradition contains numerous accounts of righteous individuals rising against idolatry: Pinchas, Eliyahu, Yirmeyahu. Meqabyan operates within the same narrative tradition but in a context unique to the Ethiopian community's historical experience. The Ge'ez text does not borrow from the Masoretic narratives but rather shares their deep structural pattern.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The mockery of Meqabyan by the apostate community — "who are you to speak to us?" — is a characteristic pattern in the ancient prophetic narrative tradition. The prophet is always initially rejected by the community he is sent to address. This pattern is not unique to any one tradition but is a universal feature of the Afro-Asiatic prophetic narrative: the authentic voice of YHWH is consistently unwelcome to those who have abandoned the covenant.

CHAPTER 2 — THE BATTLE AND THE COVENANT RENEWAL

1 And after these things the enemies of Yisra'el gathered against them, for they heard that the people had been weakened by their division and their apostasy. And they came up against the city with a great army.

2 And Meqabyan said to the people: Do not be afraid of their faces. This battle is not yours but YHWH's. If you have returned to the covenant He will fight for you. If you have not returned, no human strength will save you.

3 And the people gathered and they made a covenant before YHWH saying: We have sinned. We have abandoned Your Torah. We have bowed before idols. Forgive us and restore us and we will serve You alone from this day forward.

4 And YHWH heard their covenant and He gave them victory over the enemies that day. The enemy fell before them though they were few and the enemy was many. And the people said: Truly YHWH fights for those who keep His covenant.

5 And Meqabyan led the people in restoring the covenant. They destroyed the idols and rebuilt the altar of YHWH. They offered the proper sacrifices and restored the appointed feasts according to the ancient order.

6 And YHWH blessed them in that year and the rains came in their season and the harvest was abundant. And the people said to one another: This is the reward of covenant faithfulness. When we walk with YHWH He walks with us.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] No DSS parallel.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The covenant renewal narrative in Meqabyan follows the pattern of covenant restoration found throughout the Orit Ge'ez prophetic tradition. The sequence — apostasy, enemy threat, covenant confession, divine vindication, material blessing — is the fundamental narrative cycle of the Afro-Asiatic covenantal theology. It is present in Yovelim, in the historical books, and here in Meqabyan.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] The Masoretic Divrei HaYamim (Chronicles) presents numerous covenant renewal narratives following this same structural pattern. The Meqabyan pattern is consistent with the Masoretic historical theology without being dependent on it. Both draw from the same ancient covenantal narrative framework.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The connection between covenant faithfulness and material blessing — the rains in their season, the abundant harvest — reflects the ancient Afro-Asiatic understanding that the covenant governs the relationship between the human community and the natural order. This is not prosperity theology in the modern sense but covenantal ecology: the health of the land is connected to the moral health of the covenant community that stewards it.
